```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaGlmnet)
HAS_CUDA <- isTRUE(rcupp::cuda_available())
RUN <- HAS_CUDA
```

```{r status, echo = FALSE}
if (!RUN) {
  cat("Live timing skipped: needs a CUDA backend.\n")
}
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
make_data <- function(n, p) {
  set.seed(42)
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  list(X = X, y = rnorm(n))
}

time_median <- function(f, reps = 3L) {
  f()
  median(replicate(reps, system.time(f())[["elapsed"]]))
}

# Exact closed-form ridge for a subset, matching the C++ solver convention
# (Xs'Xs + m*lambda*I) beta = Xs'ys, with m = length(idx).
cf_beta <- function(X, y, idx, lambda) {
  Xs <- X[idx, , drop = FALSE]
  ys <- y[idx]
  m <- length(idx)
  drop(solve(crossprod(Xs) + m * lambda * diag(ncol(Xs)),
             crossprod(Xs, ys)))
}
```

`cuda_resident_subsets()` is a **composable, downstream** solver that keeps one
full panel resident on the device and refits many row subsets through a
device-side gather, without re-uploading the design matrix per subset. This
vignette measures exactly that: **data-movement amortization**, not the
performance of a closed-form ridge solver. It is a measurement, not a
performance claim, in the same spirit as the `ridge-benchmark` and
`bio-flagship-benchmark` vignettes.

## Why this matters

The `bio-flagship-benchmark` vignette showed a real but *flat* speedup: one
30-lambda resident path beats 30 cold fits (roughly 3--6x), but the ratio stays
flat as the number of candidate panels grows. The reason was stated there
honestly: `cuda_glmnet()` is a pure-R API and each call rebuilds its context
and re-uploads `X`, so refitting a *different* subset of rows still pays a full
upload every time. The `rcupp` device-context ABI had only whole-buffer
`buf_upload` / `gemv` / `ger`, with no device-side row indexing.

Stage 2 adds the missing part: `rcupp_d_gather_rows` (plus `syrk`, `potrf`,
`potrs`) lets one `rcupp_ctx` hold the whole panel once and select each subset
on the device. `cuda_resident_subsets()` composes those parts downstream
(Rcpp glue plus rcupp substrate); `rcupp` itself still carries no ridge, CV or
reference-panel code.

## What is measured

For a full panel `X` (`n x p`) and `B` equal-size row subsets (size `m`), each
subset solves the same closed-form ridge system
`(Xs'Xs + m*lambda*I) beta = Xs'ys`. Two strategies are compared:

- **resident** -- uploads the whole `n x p` panel once, then selects each
  subset with `rcupp_d_gather_rows` (device to device, no host round trip);
- **cold** -- assembles each `m x p` subset on the host and re-uploads it on
  every refit, modeling the old per-fit `set_data` cost.

Both strategies share a single `rcupp_ctx` and the same `syrk` -> `potrf` ->
`potrs` solve, so the only difference is the host-to-device transfer. That is
why the absolute cold/resident ratio here is smaller than the 3--6x of the
`bio-flagship-benchmark`: the old cold baseline there paid a fresh context and
an iterative FISTA each time, whereas here it only re-uploads. `syrk` writes
only the lower triangle, and `potrf` / `potrs` must use the same `uplo`.

## Correctness (both backends)

This chunk always runs, including on `rcupp`'s CPU reference shim: both
`rcupp_d_*` backends implement the same four parts. Resident and cold betas are
identical and match the exact closed form to machine precision.

```{r correctness}
d <- make_data(60L, 6L)
X <- d$X
y <- d$y
idx_list <- replicate(4L, sample.int(60L, 30L), simplify = FALSE)
lambda <- 0.2

res <- cuda_resident_subsets(X, y, idx_list, lambda, "resident")
cold <- cuda_resident_subsets(X, y, idx_list, lambda, "cold")

stopifnot(all(res$info == 0L), all(cold$info == 0L))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(res$beta, cold$beta, tolerance = 1e-8)))
max_cf <- max(vapply(seq_along(idx_list), function(b) {
  max(abs(res$beta[, b] - cf_beta(X, y, idx_list[[b]], lambda)))
}, numeric(1)))
stopifnot(max_cf < 1e-6)
cat(sprintf("backend cuda=%s | resident==cold | max|beta-closed form|=%.2e\n",
            res$cuda, max_cf))
```

## Reference measurement

Measured 2026-11-20 on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop GPU (8 GB), CUDA Toolkit
13.1, R 4.6.1 and cudaGlmnet 0.0.0.9011 (GPU backend). Config: `n = 12000`,
`p = 80`, `m = 6000`, `lambda = 0.1`, `B` from 1 to 32 subsets; one warm-up
then the median of repeated `system.time()` runs. Wall times in seconds; these
are a snapshot, not a performance guarantee.

| B subsets | resident (s) | cold (s) | cold / resident |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0090 | 0.0100 | 1.11x |
| 2 | 0.0120 | 0.0140 | 1.17x |
| 4 | 0.0190 | 0.0230 | 1.21x |
| 8 | 0.0280 | 0.0380 | 1.36x |
| 16 | 0.0460 | 0.0590 | 1.28x |
| 32 | 0.0780 | 0.1210 | 1.55x |

```{r roi-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
Bs <- c(1L, 2L, 4L, 8L, 16L, 32L)
res_t <- c(0.0090, 0.0120, 0.0190, 0.0280, 0.0460, 0.0780)
cold_t <- c(0.0100, 0.0140, 0.0230, 0.0380, 0.0590, 0.1210)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
plot(Bs, cold_t, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "grey40", lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, max(cold_t) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Number of subsets (B)", ylab = "Cumulative wall time (s)",
     main = "One call fitting B subsets")
lines(Bs, res_t, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("cold (re-upload)", "resident (gather)"),
       col = c("grey40", "steelblue"), pch = 19, lty = 1, bty = "n")
plot(Bs, cold_t / res_t, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(1, 1.7), xlab = "Number of subsets (B)",
     ylab = "cold / resident speedup (x)", main = "Ratio bends upward")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
par(op)
```

The resident line has a **flatter slope**: from `B = 1` to `B = 32` the
marginal cost is about `0.0022 s/subset` for resident versus `0.0036 s/subset`
for cold (roughly 1.6x). Because resident pays the full-panel upload once and
then only cheap device-side gathers, the cold/resident ratio **grows** with `B`
(from 1.11x to 1.55x) -- the flat curve from Stage 1 bends upward here for the
first time. Absolute times are small (tens of milliseconds), so individual
ratios are noisy; the reproducible signal is the slope difference, not any
single row.

```{r live-timing, eval = RUN}
cfg <- make_data(12000L, 80L)
Xb <- cfg$X
yb <- cfg$y
m <- 6000L
lam <- 0.1
Bs_live <- c(1L, 4L, 16L)
idx_live <- replicate(max(Bs_live), sample.int(12000L, m), simplify = FALSE)

rows <- lapply(Bs_live, function(B) {
  sub <- idx_live[seq_len(B)]
  t_res <- time_median(function() {
    cuda_resident_subsets(Xb, yb, sub, lam, "resident")
  }, reps = 2L)
  t_cold <- time_median(function() {
    cuda_resident_subsets(Xb, yb, sub, lam, "cold")
  }, reps = 2L)
  data.frame(
    B = B,
    resident = sprintf("%.4f", t_res),
    cold = sprintf("%.4f", t_cold),
    ratio = sprintf("%.2fx", t_cold / t_res)
  )
})

knitr::kable(
  do.call(rbind, rows),
  caption = "Device-resident subset refits (wall time, seconds)."
)
```

## Dual / Woodbury route for `p >> m`

The `p x p` primal Gram above is demo-scale. For production `p >> n` data
(e.g. a genotype panel with far more markers than samples) one solves the
algebraically equivalent **dual** system instead, via the push-through
(Woodbury) identity
`(Xs'Xs + t I)^{-1} Xs' = Xs' (Xs Xs' + t I)^{-1}` with `t = m*lambda`:
`beta = Xs' (Xs Xs' + m*lambda*I)^{-1} ys`. This builds a `m x m` system
instead of `p x p`. `cuda_resident_subsets(..., method = "dual")` composes the
C-stage `rcupp_d_gemm` part (forming `Xs Xs'`) with the B-stage `potrf` /
`potrs` parts and a final `gemv_t`; `method = "auto"` (the default) picks the
smaller system automatically -- dual when `p > m`, primal otherwise. Strategy
and method are orthogonal: `resident` / `cold` still control only data
movement.

The system dimension is the whole point, and it is deterministic (no timing
claim): for `n = 200`, `p = 4000`, `m = 150`, the primal Cholesky is `4000 x
4000` (16 million doubles ~ 128 MB) while the dual is `150 x 150` (22.5
thousand doubles ~ 0.18 MB) -- roughly 700x less memory, and a much cheaper
factorization.

| panel | p | m | primal Gram | dual Gram | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| demo | 80 | 6000 | 80 x 80 | 6000 x 6000 | dual is larger (auto picks primal) |
| genotype | 4000 | 150 | 4000 x 4000 | 150 x 150 | ~711x smaller (auto picks dual) |
| multi-omic | 2000 | 200 | 2000 x 2000 | 200 x 200 | 100x smaller (auto picks dual) |

This chunk always runs on either backend and checks that both routes agree
with each other and the exact closed form:

```{r dual-correctness}
set.seed(11)
n <- 100L
p <- 200L
m <- 40L
lambda <- 0.25
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
y <- rnorm(n)
idx <- replicate(5L, sample.int(n, m), simplify = FALSE)
exact <- vapply(idx, function(ii) cf_beta(X, y, ii, lambda), numeric(p))

auto <- cuda_resident_subsets(X, y, idx, lambda, "resident", "auto")
dual <- cuda_resident_subsets(X, y, idx, lambda, "resident", "dual")
primal <- cuda_resident_subsets(X, y, idx, lambda, "resident", "primal")
cold <- cuda_resident_subsets(X, y, idx, lambda, "cold", "dual")

stopifnot(auto$method == "dual", auto$sys_dim == m,
          primal$method == "primal", primal$sys_dim == p)
stopifnot(all(c(auto$info, dual$info, primal$info, cold$info) == 0L))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(dual$beta, primal$beta, tolerance = 1e-7)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(dual$beta, cold$beta, tolerance = 1e-10)))
max_cf <- max(abs(dual$beta - exact))
stopifnot(max_cf < 1e-6)
cat(sprintf("p=%d m=%d | method=%s sys_dim=%d | max|beta-exact|=%.2e\n",
            p, m, auto$method, auto$sys_dim, max_cf))
```

## Interpreting the numbers

This is an empirical demonstration that keeping a matrix resident and
selecting subsets on the device removes the per-subset re-upload. It is **not**
a claim that closed-form ridge is faster than `glmnet`, an iterative solver, or
a tuned dual/Woodbury solve. The `m*lambda*I` diagonal is constant across the
equal-size subsets, so it is uploaded once; `syrk` fills only the lower
triangle and `potrf` / `potrs` read that same triangle. The `method = "dual"`
route above removes the `p x p` materialization for `p >> m`, but this function
is still a reference composition, not a production tuned solver.

Read the ratio against the right baseline. Both strategies share one context
and one identical solve per subset; the resident strategy's advantage is
purely that it transforms `B` full host-to-device uploads into one upload plus
`B` device-side gathers. That advantage grows with `B` because the one upload
is amortized -- exactly the cross-subset residency that the earlier benchmarks
could not show.

The live chunk uses fewer repetitions than the reference table to keep build
time down, so its absolute numbers will differ from the snapshot for that
reason as well as for hardware differences.

## Enabling the live benchmark

The correctness chunk above always runs, on either backend. The live timing
chunk runs only when `rcupp::cuda_available()` is `TRUE`. CI runners have no
CUDA Toolkit, so `rcupp` builds its CPU reference shim there and the timing
chunk is skipped; the reference table and plot above are static snapshots from
a GPU machine. Note that the CPU shim still needs an `rcupp` built with the
B-stage parts (`gather_rows` / `syrk` / `potrf` / `potrs`); the `method =
"dual"` route additionally needs the C-stage `gemm` part. See the CUDA build
notes in the `gpu-lasso-comparison` vignette.
